title: Organizing School Materials
subtitle: The problem is never carrying it. The problem is finding it.
objectives: Set up one folder per subject and keep them separate
File a sheet the day it arrives
Pack the bag the night before
Explain why searching costs more than carrying

cards.title: Nobody loses marks for a heavy bag
cards.text: They lose them for a sheet that was in the bag the whole time and could not be found.

cards.title: A bag that packs itself
cards.text: Tap through. Rules three and four are the ones that change your mornings.

cards.title: One folder per subject, never shared
cards.text: Two subjects in one folder means every search goes through twice as much paper. Colour them if that helps.
points: **Same order in the bag** every day.

question.text: Why keep one folder per subject?
options: Every search then goes through less paper
question.explain: Searching is the cost you are trying to cut. Separating subjects halves it immediately.

cards.title: File it the day it arrives
cards.text: An unfiled sheet in a bag gets handled three more times. Then it is lost.
points: **Into the right folder** on the same day.

cards.title: Inventory management is a real skill
cards.text: In any survival game, the players who die are the ones sorting their inventory at the wrong moment.
points: **A full bag is not the problem.**

question.text: A loose sheet in the bottom of a bag is fine as long as you know it is there.
question.explain: You will handle it several more times and then lose it. File it the day it arrives.

cards.title: Halfway
cards.text: Part 2 is the night-before pack and the weekly reset. Take a break.

cards.title: Morning you is not the person to trust with this
cards.text: Everything about a school morning is rushed. Every decision you can move to the night before is a decision you win.

cards.title: One place, by the door
cards.text: Bag, shoes and water bottle live in the same spot every night. Nothing is searched for at 6:40 in the morning.

cards.title: A pit crew rehearses the boring part
cards.text: Everything is laid out before the car arrives. Nobody is looking for a wheel gun while the clock runs.

cards.title: Empty it completely, once a week
cards.text: Take everything out. Bin the rubbish, file the paper, put back only what belongs.
points: **A bag that is never emptied** fills with sediment.

question.text: What should a weekly clear-out involve?
options: Moving everything to a bigger bag
Emptying the bag completely, then putting back only what belongs
question.explain: Complete emptying is the point. Otherwise old paper settles at the bottom and stays.

cards.title: This is not about being tidy
cards.text: Some brains find it hard to hold several things at once. That system belongs outside your head.

terms.def: Putting a sheet in its folder the day it arrives.
The one place bag, shoes and bottle live overnight.
Emptying the bag completely and putting back only what belongs.
Deal with a piece of paper the first time you touch it.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Pack the night before**, at one spot.

quiz.text: What is the main cost of a disorganised bag?
quiz.explain: Nobody loses marks for a heavy bag. They lose them for a sheet they could not find.
quiz.objective: Explain why searching costs more than carrying

quiz.text: How many subjects should share one folder?
quiz.explain: Two subjects in one folder doubles the paper every search has to go through.
quiz.objective: Set up one folder per subject and keep them separate

quiz.text: Where should a folder be labelled?
options: It does not need a label
quiz.explain: A label you have to open the folder to read does not save you a search.
quiz.objective: Set up one folder per subject and keep them separate

quiz.text: When should a new sheet be filed?
options: At the end of the term
When a teacher asks for it
quiz.explain: Handle paper once. Unfiled paper gets handled several more times and then lost.
quiz.objective: File a sheet the day it arrives

quiz.text: Handling a piece of paper once is faster overall than dealing with it later.
quiz.explain: True. Two seconds now saves the several handlings and the eventual search.
quiz.objective: File a sheet the day it arrives

quiz.text: When should the bag be packed?
quiz.explain: Prepare when it is cheap. A school morning is the expensive part of the day.
quiz.objective: Pack the bag the night before

options: The first classroom of the day
The one place bag, shoes and bottle live overnight
quiz.explain: One place, chosen once, so nothing is searched for at 6:40 in the morning.
quiz.objective: Pack the bag the night before

quiz.text: What should you check while packing the night before?
quiz.explain: Packing to the actual timetable is what keeps the bag from becoming everything you own.
quiz.objective: Pack the bag the night before

quiz.text: What does a weekly reset involve?
options: Emptying the bag completely and refilling it deliberately
Wiping the outside of the bag
quiz.explain: Complete emptying is the point, and it takes about four minutes.

quiz.text: How many spare pens is the rule suggesting?
quiz.explain: One spare, kept separately. A drawer of spares is just more clutter.

quiz.text: Organising your materials is mostly about willpower and being naturally tidy.
quiz.explain: False. It is about building a system outside your head so you need less discipline, not more.
quiz.objective: Explain why searching costs more than carrying

quiz.text: Why sort your bag when nothing urgent is happening?
options: Sorting under pressure is when things go wrong
quiz.explain: Same principle as inventory management in a game: prepare when it is cheap.
quiz.objective: Explain why searching costs more than carrying

teacher.summary: Week 7 is the school-materials half of the TLE organisation strand, and it deliberately does not moralise about tidiness. The framing throughout is cost: searching is expensive, carrying is not, and every rule here reduces search. The last lens card names the ADHD reality directly and reframes the whole week as building an external system rather than trying harder — which is both true and the only version of this advice that tends to stick. The weekly reset is the single highest-value habit in the lesson and is deliberately given a duration, because 'four minutes' is startable and 'sort your bag' is not.
discussion: Ask him to time one actual search for a specific sheet. The number usually makes the argument.
Ask which of the six rules he already does without thinking about it.
Ask where the launch spot should be, and let him choose it.
Ask what would have to be true for the weekly reset to actually happen every week.
teacher.extension: Have him set up the folders and run the night-before pack for five school days, then report what broke. Something always does, and fixing it is the real lesson.
misconceptions: 'A big bag solves it.' More space just means more unsorted material.
'I will file it later.' Later means handling the same sheet several more times before losing it.
'Being organised means being naturally tidy.' It means having a system that needs no memory.
'One clear-out fixes it.' Without the weekly reset, the bag refills with sediment in a fortnight.
